Direct-acting (or “direct-acting”) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the incoming electricity into heat at the point of use, so in that very narrow sense they are fully efficient. However, when assessing their overall energy performance and running costs you need to look at two further factors:

1. Primary-energy efficiency  
   – Electricity generation (even from renewables) and grid transmission involve losses. If you compare “wall-to-wall” efficiency — from fuel extraction or power-plant input to heat output in your room — direct electric heating typically has a higher primary-energy factor than, say, a modern air-source or ground-source heat pump.  
   – In many EPC (energy performance certificate) schemes, buildings solely heated by direct electric radiators often score towards the lower end of the energy-class scale (e.g. classes E, F or G).

2. Operating cost and carbon footprint  
   – Electricity tariffs are generally more expensive per kWh of heat delivered

Here are several practical measures to get the best performance and lowest running costs from direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Fit a room thermostat or programmable radiator controls  
   • Use digital thermostats (built-in or individual) to regulate each room’s temperature rather than running all radiators full-blast.  
   • Program lower set-points at night or when rooms are unoccupied, and higher set-points only for periods of use.  

2. Zone your heating  
   • Divide your home into “comfort” and “eco” zones. Keep radiators in living rooms and bedrooms on a normal schedule, but turn down or switch off radiators in corridors, guest rooms or storage areas.  
   • If possible, install smart or Wi-Fi-enabled thermostatic radiator valves to control each radiator independently.

3. Optimize thermostat set-points  
   • A reduction of 1 °C typically cuts energy consumption by 5–10 %. Find the lowest comfortable level (often between 18 °C and 20 °C) before increasing to higher levels.

Natural (or passive) ventilation relies on wind pressure and thermal buoyancy to move fresh air through a building, rather than fans or ducts. Compared with mechanical ventilation, its main advantages are:

1. Lower energy use and operating costs  
   • No or minimal fan-power consumption.  
   • Reduced electricity bills, especially in mild climates or transitional seasons.  
   • Smaller carbon footprint since you’re not running motors continuously.

2. Simplified installation and maintenance  
   • Fewer mechanical components (fans, motors, filters, ductwork) to install.  
   • Lower capital expenditure on equipment.  
   • Minimal ongoing maintenance—no periodic motor servicing or complex filter changes.

3. Enhanced reliability and resilience  
   • Continues to operate in power outages or system failures.  
   • No risk of fan breakdowns or control-system malfunctions.  
   • Simpler building services reduce risk of unexpected downtime.

Here are some of the main advantages of installing solar panels on a building:

1. Lower energy bills  
   • Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity you can use in the building, reducing your reliance on grid‐supplied power.  
   • Any surplus electricity you generate can often be sold back to the grid (net metering), further cutting your overall costs.

2. Environmental benefits  
   • Solar energy is a renewable, zero-emission power source—installing panels reduces your carbon footprint and helps combat climate change.  
   • You avoid burning fossil fuels and the associated air pollution, contributing to better local air quality.

3. Energy independence and security  
   • Generating your own electricity makes you less vulnerable to utility price hikes and power outages (especially if paired with battery storage).  
   • In remote locations or areas with an unreliable grid, solar can provide a stable, on-site power supply.

Load balancing for electric-vehicle (EV) charging is a strategy—often implemented in hardware, software or both—to distribute the available electrical capacity intelligently across one or more charging points. Its goal is to maximize the use of a site’s existing electrical supply without tripping breakers or forcing costly grid upgrades.

In Sweden there is no universal “one-size-fits-all” set-point for stairwells, but the general guidance is:

• Minimum design temperature  
  – The heating system must be sized so that—even at the dimensioning outdoor temperature—the stairwell never drops below about +10 °C to +12 °C (this prevents frost damage, condensation and mould).  

• Usual set-point for comfort  
  – In practice most housing companies choose a constant thermostat setting of +15 °C to +18 °C. That range strikes a balance between keeping the space frost-protected and avoiding unnecessary energy use.  

If your building has special requirements (for example a healthcare facility or a cultural heritage object) you should always check the applicable Boverket regulations (BBR) or any other sector-specific norms.

Practical tips:
